content: Conversion from an HIV-negative antibody test result to a positive test result is sometimes used as a proxy for estimating seroincidence. Various methods for estimating this measure are described, including CD4/AIDS back-calculation, retesting, recency testing, routine antenatal HIV testing, age-specific HIV prevalence, phylogenetics, and the inclusion of routine data in modeling. CD4/AIDS Back-Calculation: Back-calculation is a widely used method to estimate the number of newly acquired HIV infections over time, or HIV incidence, based on observed longitudinal data on HIV or AIDS diagnoses. The principle behind back-calculation is that if the progression of a biomarker, such as CD4 cell counts, during untreated HIV infection is well-characterized, the biomarker levels at the time of diagnosis can be used to estimate the time since acquiring the HIV infection. This method is particularly useful in settings with concentrated HIV epidemics, where it may be the only available approach for estimating HIV incidence. Initially, back-calculation relied on the observed number of AIDS diagnoses and the known incubation period of AIDS (the time from infection to AIDS-related clinical symptoms in the absence of treatment). However, with the advent of effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), back-calculation methods now primarily use data on HIV diagnoses, although information on concurrent AIDS-defining events at the time of HIV diagnosis can still be utilized. Using HIV diagnoses allows for greater precision in estimating the HIV incidence curve, as the time to HIV diagnosis is generally much shorter than the time to AIDS. CD4 cell counts at diagnosis are the most important biomarker used for back-calculation and are often available as routinely collected data for new diagnoses. Most untreated individuals with HIV experience a steady decline in CD4 cell counts over time. The rate of CD4 decline is well-documented from cohorts of individuals with a known date of HIV seroconversion and is influenced by factors such as age, gender, ethnicity, and HIV viral load. When an individual is diagnosed with HIV and has a CD4 cell count measurement, the time since acquiring HIV can be estimated using the known distribution of times to reach that CD4 count level. Lower CD4 counts are indicative of a longer duration since infection. Importantly, the CD4 measurement must be taken before the initiation of treatment, as CD4 counts typically increase after treatment begins. In settings where CD4 counts at diagnosis are not available for all individuals, statistical methods can be used to impute CD4 values based on characteristics of individuals with and without CD4 measurements. These characteristics may include demographic information (e.g., age, gender, nationality, and residence) and clinical information (e.g., HIV viral load at diagnosis and the date of the last HIV-negative test). Data from other settings on the rate of CD4 decline over time may also be used when local data are unavailable. Challenges may arise when retesting of known HIV-positive individuals cannot be deduplicated, potentially biasing estimates of the time of infection. Other clinical information, such as viral load or the presence of antiretroviral drugs in the blood, can help differentiate new diagnoses from known HIV-positive individuals who retest. Case Study: Estimating HIV Incidence in Brazil In Brazil, the Ministry of Health updates a linked database annually with data from four main information systems related to HIV: SINAN (Notifiable Disease Information System), SIM (Mortality Information System), SISCEL (Laboratory Test Control System), and SICLOM (System for Logistic Control of ARV Drugs). This integrated HIV information system is used for both patient monitoring and case surveillance. To estimate HIV incidence, a back-calculation method is applied using the first CD4 count among ART-naïve individuals living with HIV, as reported in the HIV information system. The Brazilian CD4 depletion model is used to estimate the time between infection and the first CD4 count, as well as the time between infection and diagnosis. For cases without CD4 count information, a multiple imputation procedure is used to estimate the time between infection and diagnosis based on notification criteria. HIV incidence is calculated as the cumulative sum of individuals living with HIV reported in the same year of infection, the year following infection, and subsequent years. However, as the accuracy of incidence estimates decreases with smaller numbers of observations, recent estimates have relied on the number of cases diagnosed within the first year of infection. A regression model predicts the proportion of cases reported within the first year of infection, and the incidence estimate is derived from the ratio of newly infected individuals diagnosed within the first year to the predicted proportion. In 2021, the model was adapted to estimate HIV incidence at granular levels, including region of residence, age group, and sex. The approach is applicable to all countries that monitor clinical information, such as CD4 counts and ART initiation. Retesting for HIV: Retesting for HIV plays a critical role in sustaining prevention activities, particularly in high-burden settings. It provides opportunities to engage or re-engage individuals testing HIV-negative and facilitates re-linkage to care for those who are HIV-positive. Frequent retesting among priority groups, such as key populations for whom annual testing is recommended, promotes earlier diagnosis among individuals who have acquired HIV since their last negative test. The decision to retest is influenced by factors such as awareness of HIV status, female gender, knowing someone living with HIV, recognition of ongoing elevated risk, and the use of opt-out HIV testing approaches. Some individuals with known HIV-positive status also retest, including those already on treatment. Reasons for non-disclosure of HIV-positive status and retesting may include stigma, discrimination, denial, or a lack of understanding of an HIV diagnosis. Retesting as an intervention can identify new infections, reducing missed or delayed opportunities for diagnosis. By shortening the period between infection and diagnosis, retesting reduces the risk of disease progression and associated morbidity and mortality. However, as retesting is associated with declining HIV test positivity rates, it is important to monitor changing testing patterns and consider their influence when interpreting these rates. Among individuals testing HIV-positive, median CD4 counts are higher among those retesting compared to first-time testers. Retesting has been linked to reductions in HIV diagnoses among certain populations, such as gay and bisexual men in London, prior to the scale-up of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Retesting also facilitates re-entry into care for individuals previously diagnosed with HIV, reducing their risk of advanced disease and high viral load. To improve the accuracy of HIV diagnoses, prevalence, and incidence estimates, it is essential to capture longitudinal testing data and address duplicate positive results. Strategies include validating self-reports with medical records, linking information across sites, and incorporating additional data sources into surveillance systems. Unique personal identifiers that work across multiple health services can enhance data tracking and deduplication. Self-Testing and Retesting: Self-testing has potential as an additional retesting tool but is currently limited by affordability and accessibility. Further exploration is needed to determine how self-reported data on self-testing could be incorporated into retesting analyses.
